blogs.title: The 'Listener' as a Recipient: Interpreting Statutory 'Receipt' in the Age of APIs
blogs.description: This post explores the 5th Circuit’s modern interpretation of 'receipt' in the context of automated insurance cancellation. By holding that a computer system 'listening' for an API call satisfies the statutory requirement for 'taking possession,' the court signals a technology-neutral approach to commerce law. We will discuss the implications of this ruling for other industries where automated 'web services' replace human intermediaries, and how courts should reconcile 20th-century language with 21st-century infrastructure.

blogs.title: When 'Strict Adherence' Isn't a License for Judicial Invention
blogs.description: While the Louisiana statute requires 'strict adherence' to cancellation procedures, the 5th Circuit refused to read a physical signature requirement into the law. This post analyzes the tension between a court's duty to ensure compliance and the textualist principle that judges cannot add requirements to a statute that doesn't expressly include them. It examines the court's reasoning that 'certifying' does not inherently necessitate a signature, offering a cautionary note for plaintiffs seeking to expand statutory duties through judicial interpretation.

blogs.title: The High Price of Certification: Why 'Undefined' Isn't 'Compelling'
blogs.description: In a move of judicial restraint, the 5th Circuit declined to certify the interpretation of Louisiana's insurance statutes to the state's high court. This post analyzes the circuit's 'scarcity' theory of certification—the idea that the power to certify is a precious resource that should not be spent merely because a state supreme court hasn't yet weighed in on a specific term. We will explore the standard for 'compelling reasons' and what this means for litigants trying to move questions of state law into the supreme court's orbit.
